name: Council of Basel–Ferrara–Florence
region: Basel, on the Rhine; then Ferrara and Florence; later Rome
teaser: Basel, 1431; Ferrara and Florence, 1438 and 1439. A council that began at Basel was moved by Pope Eugenius IV to meet the Greeks. At Florence, Latins and Greeks signed a decree of union.
knownFor: The council at which the Greek emperor and bishops signed a union with Rome in 1439. Doukas says the bishops told the people at home, "We have sold our faith."
datesNote: 1431 to 1445, the span the councils scan gives. Basel opened on 23 July 1431, by its acts as Raynaldus quotes them. Glassberger dates its first session to Friday 7 December 1431; his Quaracchi editors give 14 December, after Hergenröther and Brück. On 7 May 1437 the fathers split over where to meet the Greeks. Mansi's note says two rival decrees came out of the same session. Eugenius's bull moving the council to Ferrara is dated 18 September 1437 by Raynaldus and by Mansi. Mansi says the acts printed by Justiniani wrongly read 1 October. Ferrara opened on Wednesday 8 January 1438, by the record Raynaldus quotes. The solemn opening with the Greeks was on 9 April 1438, by the Greek acts and Eugenius's decree. Eugenius's decree moved the council to Florence on 10 January 1439. It is dated 1438 because the year was counted from the Incarnation. The decree of union was signed on 5 July 1439 and read on 6 July. Later the council moved to Rome. Patrizi puts that session in April 1442, and Mansi argues for 1441. Denzinger's heading gives 1438–1445 for Florence, and Mansi's tomus 35 gives 1438–1446. No held act names a closing session. Those who stayed at Basel deposed Eugenius on 25 June 1439. Only Glassberger gives the day they elected Felix V, 17 November 1439. By Mansi's note, the Basel party moved to Lausanne in 1448 and ended there in April 1449.
issue: Basel was to end the Hussite heresy, Glassberger says. Eugenius IV confirmed Cardinal Julian Cesarini as legate for the council, "above all to root out the heresy of the Hussites." The Taborite chronicle says Basel invited the Bohemians to a free hearing. Their envoys set out their Four Articles before the whole council in 1433.

Council against pope. Glassberger says the Basel fathers held, by the decrees of Constance renewed at Basel, that a lawful general council had its power directly from Christ. It stood above the pope, they said, so he could not move or dissolve it without its consent. Bannwart, Denzinger's editor, notes that Eugenius rejected the Constance teaching on 4 September 1439.

Where to meet the Greeks. Bissipatus, envoy of the Greek emperor, told Basel in 1437 that the place must suit the pope too. His presence, he said, was needed above all, and nothing good could come without it (in Raynaldus). Raynaldus says Basel's majority wanted Basel, Avignon or a town in Savoy. Mansi's note says the papal legates' party chose Florence, Udine or another town.

The Turks. The anonymous Roman history printed before the Greek acts says Turkish force squeezed the eastern empire tighter every day. The chronicle printed under Sphrantzes's name has Manuel II tell his son that the Turks feared a union of Greeks and Latins. He told him to keep the council in mind while the Turks were a danger, but not to hold it. He feared a worse schism. John rose and left without a word. Chalkokondyles says the pope at Ferrara asked the emperor to help him in his quarrel with the Germans, that is, with Basel.

The doctrine. The Roman history lists the procession of the Holy Spirit and the Filioque, unleavened bread, purgatory, the saints' vision of God and the pope's primacy. Petit, the modern editor, says purgatory came first, at private meetings from April 1438. Mark of Ephesus says the first public debate was on the words added to the Creed, then the doctrine itself at Florence.

Why the Greeks came is told by witnesses, and no decree states a bargain. Mark of Ephesus wrote that the city was being guarded "by the Pope's gold." The later Greek chronicle printed by Bekker says no help was sent afterwards.
calledBy: Basel was opened under Martin V and Eugenius IV by two delegates of Cardinal Julian Cesarini, by its acts as Raynaldus quotes them. Glassberger says Martin V sent Cesarini to begin it. Eugenius IV moved the council to Ferrara and called the Greeks there, Raynaldus says. Eugenius's decree at Ferrara says the emperor and the patriarch consented. His decree moving it to Florence names their consent too, "with the approval of the holy council." Patrizi says Eugenius moved it to Rome in a session at Florence.
attended: No full roll of Basel is among our sources. Mansi's note says that at the opening no bishops were there, only a few abbots.

Ferrara's first session, on 8 January 1438, had five archbishops, eighteen bishops, four bishops-elect and many heads of religious orders, Raynaldus says. Cardinal Nicholas Albergati presided for the pope.

The emperor John VIII Palaiologos and Patriarch Joseph II of Constantinople came with the Greek bishops. Syropoulos lists the bishops of twenty sees, from Ephesus and Trebizond to Moldo-Wallachia and Rhodes. Isidore came from Russia with one bishop. Envoys of the patriarchs of Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem came too, by the Roman history.
Syropoulos says the emperor's man brought two bishops and an envoy from Georgia. Later he speaks of one Georgian bishop and one lay prince.
Doukas names among the Greeks Mark of Ephesus, Bessarion of Nicaea, Isidore, George Scholarios and Gemistos of Lacedaemon. Mark spoke for the Greeks and Cardinal Julian for the Latins, he says.

The signed list of the decree of union is held in Mansi's tomus 31. Our count finds more than a hundred Latin and about thirty Greek signatures in the printed list. The pope signs first, then eight cardinals, Latin patriarchs, bishops, envoys of Burgundy and heads of orders. On the Greek side, the emperor signs first, then the metropolitans and envoys of the eastern patriarchs, then officials and monks.
The Roman editor of the list says many fathers had left before the signing, so their names are missing.

At Basel's session that deposed Eugenius, Raynaldus counts only seven bishops. He quotes Aeneas Silvius, who was there. Aeneas says no Spanish or Aragonese prelate came, and from Italy only the bishop of Grosseto and one abbot.
Later envoys came from the Armenians in 1439 and from the Copts and the Ethiopians in 1441. The Syrians came in 1444, and the Chaldeans and Maronites of Cyprus in 1445 (Raynaldus; the decrees).
decided: Eugenius's decree of 9 April 1438 declared the ecumenical synod to be at Ferrara, with the emperor and patriarch consenting (the Greek acts). Asked if they received it, both sides answered, "We receive and approve."

Against Basel. Ferrara's first session ruled that those staying at Basel under the council's name had incurred the penalties of the transfer. It called their meeting a conventicle (in Raynaldus). On 4 September 1439, at Florence, the decree Moyses condemned Basel's teaching and its attempt to depose the pope (in Raynaldus).

The decree of union Laetentur caeli, read on 6 July 1439 (the acts, in Mansi; extracts in Denzinger and Mirbt). It begins: "Let the heavens rejoice and the earth be glad: the wall that divided the western and the eastern church has been taken away."

It taught that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as from one principle and one spiration. The fathers' phrase, "from the Father through the Son," was read in that sense. It said the word Filioque had been added to the Creed lawfully and with good reason.
It allowed the eucharist in unleavened or leavened wheat bread, each priest following his own church, western or eastern. It taught purgatory and the soul's vision of God after death.

It gave the apostolic see and the Roman pontiff primacy over the whole world. It called the pope true vicar of Christ and head of the whole church. It set the order of the patriarchs, "saving all their privileges and rights." The Greek acts say the Latins tried to drop the word "all."

The decree for the Armenians, Exultate Deo, dated 22 November 1439 (the acts, in Mansi). It gave them the Creed with the Filioque, the faith of Chalcedon, the seven sacraments and Latin feast dates. The envoys accepted it in their own name, their patriarch's and that of all Armenians.

The decree for the Copts, Cantate Domino, dated 4 February 1442 by our reckoning (in Raynaldus). It rejoices that "before three years have passed" three great nations have been joined. Andrew, abbot of Saint Antony's in Egypt, accepted it for Patriarch John and his people.

In a Lateran session on 30 September 1444, Abdallah, archbishop of Edessa, accepted the faith for Ignatius, patriarch of the Syrians (in Raynaldus). The decree says he had read the decrees for the Greeks, Armenians and Copts in Arabic.

The bull Benedictus sit Deus of 7 August 1445 received two men from Cyprus (in Raynaldus). They were Timothy, metropolitan of the Chaldeans, and Isaac, sent by Elias, bishop of the Maronites. It gave them the rights of other Catholics.

At Basel, after the split, the fathers set out three propositions on a council's power and deposed Eugenius. Raynaldus calls the propositions false. They elected Felix V and defined the Immaculate Conception (Glassberger). Glassberger's modern editors say that definition never bound the faith, since it was not the act of a lawful council.
outcome: Bessarion and Isidore were made cardinals, Chalkokondyles says.

Doukas, a Greek historian of the fall, says people met the returning bishops at the harbor and asked, "Did we win?" They answered, "We have sold our faith, we have traded piety for impiety." He says Antony of Heraclea and others who had signed spoke like this.
Doukas, who favored the union, also says some bishops would not sign until they were paid. Syropoulos says the opposite: no money was asked or promised at the signing.

Mark of Ephesus led the refusal at home. In his letter to the faithful he calls the unionists "Graeco-Latins," half-beasts like the centaurs. "What union is this," he asks, "where no plain sign appears?" To Scholarios he wrote, "Between truth and falsehood there is nothing in between."
Petit, the modern editor, says the new patriarch Metrophanes proclaimed the union in the islands in June and July 1440.

Mansi's tomus 35 prints a decree of 1443 in which the patriarchs of Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem condemn Metrophanes and the union. Mansi thinks it a forgery by a Greek partisan. Mouravieff, a Russian writer of 1838, tells it as fact (see uncertain).

In Moscow, Mouravieff says, Isidore had the acts of Florence proclaimed in the cathedral of the Dormition. Grand Prince Basil called him a traitor. The bishops would not own the pope as Vicar of Christ and rejected the Filioque. Isidore was confined in the Chudov monastery and escaped to Rome. Harasiewicz, a Ruthenian Catholic writing in 1862, also says Basil opposed the union. Both are later narratives.

In Constantinople the union was celebrated on 12 December 1452, Leonard of Chios writes, "if it was not feigned." Doukas says Scholarios, now the monk Gennadios, posted a warning on his cell door. After the union, Doukas says, people shunned Hagia Sophia like a synagogue of the Jews.
Issaverdens, a modern Armenian Catholic historian, says the catholicos Constantine sent four vardapets, who accepted and signed the union.
The Ethiopian chronicles of Zara Yaqob say nothing of Florence, Perruchon, their editor, notes.

The Basel party went on to Lausanne. Felix V gave up his title on 7 April 1449, by Mansi's note. In its decree of 16 April 1449, the Lausanne synod still said it had been lawfully gathered at Basel. It had not consented, it said, when Eugenius set up a meeting at Ferrara under a council's name. The French envoys' instrument of 4 April 1449 speaks of Pope Nicholas V's wish for peace.
In 1516 the Fifth Lateran Council called Basel after the transfer a "little council, or rather a gathering" (in Mirbt). It no longer deserved the name of council, Lateran said.

The Roman history printed before the acts says the Greeks never received this council, apart from those who sat in it. The Greeks call it the eighth, it adds. The Greek chronicle printed by Bekker also calls it the eighth synod. It came to no good end, it says, because Mark of Ephesus refused to sign, and many quarreled again at home.

record.witness: The Greek acts, with a Latin version (Mansi, tomus 31)
record.note: A first-person record by a Greek delegate, from the voyage to the reading of the decree. Mansi does not name the writer. Petit gives him, in brackets, as Dorotheos of Mitylene. Pro-union in outcome.

record.witness: Laetentur caeli with its signatures; Eugenius's decree at Ferrara; Patriarch Joseph's last statement; Exultate Deo (Mansi, tomus 31)
record.note: The council's own texts. Joseph's statement is given as the Greek acts report it.

record.witness: Laetentur caeli, Exultate Deo and Cantate Domino in Denzinger (ed. Bannwart) and Mirbt
record.note: Modern editors' extracts. They date Cantate Domino 1441 by the Florentine year.

record.witness: Letters of the council of Basel, the Compacts with the Bohemians and bulls of Felix V (Mansi, tomus 31, appendices)
record.note: Basel's own documents, printed by Mansi from manuscripts. For the Basel party.

record.witness: The decree of the Lausanne synod, 1449, and the French envoys' instrument (Mansi, tomus 32)
record.note: Acts of the Basel party at its end; it speaks for itself against Eugenius.

record.witness: Mansi, tomus 35: additions to the council of Florence
record.note: The Armenian envoys' address and the 1443 decree of the eastern patriarchs, which Mansi thinks forged.

record.witness: Sylvester Syropoulos, memoir (Vera historia unionis non verae, ed. Creyghton, 1660)
record.note: A Greek delegate, great ecclesiarch of Constantinople, who signed the decree. His memoir is hostile to the union. The main witness for the scene at Ferrara.

record.witness: Mark of Ephesus, account of his acts at Florence and letter to the faithful (in Petit's Documents, PO 17); letter to Scholarios (PG 160)
record.note: The one Greek bishop who openly refused to sign, in his own words. Against the union.

record.witness: Bessarion, works (PG 161); Mark and Bessarion on purgatory (in Petit, PO 15)
record.note: Bessarion was a Greek spokesman who read the decree in Greek. For the union.

record.witness: John of Ragusa, report to the council of Basel on his embassy to Constantinople (Mansi, tomus 31)
record.note: Basel's envoy to the Greeks; for Basel.

record.witness: Raynaldus, Annales ecclesiastici, tomus 28 (ed. Theiner), with Mansi's notes
record.note: A Roman annalist of the 17th century. He quotes the acts of Basel's opening, Eugenius's letters and decrees, Aeneas Silvius and the later decrees of union. Papal side; he calls the Basel party schismatics.

record.witness: Nicholas Glassberger, Chronica
record.note: A Franciscan chronicler writing in 1508. For Basel's aims, its doctrine of a council's power, the deposition and Felix V.

record.witness: Chronicon Taboritarum of Nicholas of Pelhřimov and John of Lukavec (in Höfler)
record.note: Taborite; for Basel's hearing of the Bohemians in 1433.

record.witness: Doukas, Historia Byzantina, with the editors' notes
record.note: Greek historian of the fall of Constantinople. His first editor, Boulliau, says he held to communion with the Catholic church. He scorns those at home who rejected the union. The notes correct him from the acts.

record.witness: The chronicle printed under Sphrantzes's name; Laonikos Chalkokondyles, Histories; Leonard of Chios (PG 159)
record.note: Greek and Latin writers of the fall. Leonard, a Latin, doubts the union of 1452 was meant.

record.witness: Historia politica et patriarchica Constantinopoleos (ed. Bekker, in Crusius's Latin)
record.note: A Greek chronicle of Constantinople running to 1578. Calls Florence the eighth synod; against its outcome.

record.witness: A. N. Mouravieff, History of the Church of Russia (1838; English, 1842); Harasiewicz, Annales ecclesiae Ruthenae (1862)
record.note: Mouravieff writes for the Russian Orthodox side, Harasiewicz for the Ruthenian Catholic. Both are late.

record.witness: Issaverdens, Armenia and the Armenians (1875); Perruchon, the chronicles of Zara Yaqob (1893)
record.note: Modern writers on the Armenian and Ethiopian sides.

record.witness: Hiob Ludolf, Commentarius ad Historiam Aethiopicam (1691), with a Latin version of the oration of the Portuguese patriarch Alphonsus Mendez
record.note: Ludolf says Zara Yaqob stood apart from the Roman church. The oration, in his Latin, says the emperor and the metropolitan sent the envoys.

record.witness: Manuel de Almeida, Historia Aethiopiae, books V-VIII (ed. Beccari), with Mendez's oration of 1626 in Portuguese
record.note: Jesuit history of the mission, for the Roman side. Its text of the oration says the emperor and the patriarch sent the envoys.

record.witness: Alphonsus Mendez, Expeditio Aethiopica, books I-II (ed. Beccari), with Innocent X's brief of 1645
record.note: The patriarch's own history. Beccari's introduction calls Zara Yaqob's obedience at Florence a fiction.

record.witness: Mansi, Petit, Bannwart, Mirbt, Glassberger's Quaracchi editors and Perruchon citing Dillmann
record.note: Editors who fix the dates of the transfer, of the move to Rome and of the Coptic decree. They also judge the 1443 synod and name the Ethiopians' sender.

traditions.name: The Latin Papal Church (Avignon to Fifth Lateran)
traditions.note: Eugenius IV moved the council to Ferrara and signed the decree of union first (Raynaldus; the signed list).

traditions.name: The Latin Papal Church (Avignon to Fifth Lateran)
traditions.note: Those who stayed at Basel deposed Eugenius and elected Felix V, and the split lasted until 1449 (Glassberger; Mansi's note; the Lausanne decree).

traditions.name: The Byzantine Church, Palaiologan Era
traditions.note: The emperor, the patriarch and the bishops came. About thirty Greeks signed, the emperor first (the Greek acts; the signed list).

traditions.name: The Byzantine Church, Palaiologan Era
traditions.note: At home, Doukas says, bishops who had signed disowned it, and the people shunned Hagia Sophia after the union of 1452. Mark of Ephesus led the refusal in his letters.

traditions.name: Armenian Christianity after the Kingdom (Sis to Etchmiadzin)
traditions.note: The catholicos's envoys accepted the decree Exultate Deo for all Armenians in 1439 (the acts; Issaverdens).

traditions.name: The Ethiopian Monastic Flowering
traditions.note: Ethiopian envoys came to Florence and Rome in 1441 (Raynaldus). Who sent them is disputed: Eugenius and Perruchon name the emperor, Dillmann the abbot of the Ethiopians in Jerusalem.

traditions.name: Maronite Christianity — the Union Formalized
traditions.note: Isaac, sent by Elias, bishop of the Maronites of Cyprus, was received in a Lateran session in 1445 (Raynaldus).

traditions.name: The Church of the East — Timur's Catastrophe and the Northern Remnant
traditions.note: Timothy, metropolitan of the Chaldeans of Cyprus, professed the Catholic faith in 1445 (Raynaldus). The census entry is the nearest fit for this island community.

traditions.name: The Franciscan Order — Spirituals Crisis to the Great Division
traditions.note: The general of the Friars Minor signed the decree of union (the signed list). The friar Albert carried the pope's letters to the Copts (Raynaldus).

traditions.name: Muscovite Monastic Christianity
traditions.note: Grand Prince Basil and the Russian bishops rejected Isidore and the union, by Mouravieff and Harasiewicz, both later writers.

traditions.name: The Hussite & Bohemian Brethren Movement
traditions.note: Basel invited the Bohemians and heard their Four Articles in 1433 (the Taborite chronicle).

people.name: Eugenius IV
people.part: Pope; moved the council to Ferrara, Florence and Rome; signed the decree first; asked whether Mark had signed (Syropoulos)

people.name: John VIII Palaiologos
people.part: Emperor; led the Greeks and signed first for them; would not let the pope judge Mark (Syropoulos)

people.name: Joseph II of Constantinople
people.part: Patriarch; refused to kiss the pope's foot, by Syropoulos; died at Florence in June 1439, leaving a written statement of faith (the Greek acts)

people.name: Mark of Ephesus (Mark Eugenikos)
people.part: Greek spokesman; refused to sign; led the refusal at home in his letters

people.name: Bessarion
people.part: Metropolitan of Nicaea; Greek spokesman; read the decree in Greek and signed; made a cardinal

people.name: Gennadios Scholarios (George Scholarios)
people.part: Present, by Doukas; later, as the monk Gennadios, warned against the union of 1452

people.name: Sylvester Syropoulos
people.part: Great ecclesiarch; signed the decree; wrote the memoir hostile to the union

people.name: Isidore of Kiev
people.part: Metropolitan from Russia; signed for Antioch; made a cardinal; rejected in Moscow, by Mouravieff

people.name: Gregory Mammas
people.part: Hieromonk and protosyncellus; signed for Alexandria; later wrote against Mark

people.name: Georgios Gemistos Plethon
people.part: Present, by Doukas

people.name: Julian Cesarini
people.part: Cardinal; legate for Basel at its start; Latin spokesman; read the decree in Latin

people.name: Nicholas Albergati
people.part: Cardinal; presided at Ferrara's first session (Raynaldus)

people.name: Louis Aleman, Cardinal of Arles
people.part: Led Basel's majority and the session that deposed Eugenius (Raynaldus)

people.name: Felix V (Amadeus of Savoy)
people.part: Elected pope by Basel in 1439 (Glassberger); gave up the title in 1449 (Mansi's note)

people.name: Nicholas V
people.part: Not present; pope when the Basel party made peace in 1449 (the French envoys' instrument)

people.name: Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini
people.part: At Basel; eyewitness of the session that deposed Eugenius, as Raynaldus quotes him

people.name: John of Ragusa
people.part: Dominican; opened Basel as one of Cesarini's two delegates (the acts in Raynaldus); later Basel's envoy to Constantinople; his report to Basel is in Mansi

people.name: Antony of Heraclea
people.part: Metropolitan; first Greek prelate to sign, for Alexandria; at home said they had sold their faith (Doukas)

people.name: Dorotheos of Mitylene
people.part: Metropolitan; signed; went over to the Latins, by Syropoulos; author of the Greek acts, by Petit's bracketed attribution

people.name: Metrophanes of Cyzicus
people.part: Metropolitan; signed; patriarch from 1440

people.name: Isaias of Stauropolis
people.part: Bishop; slipped away from Florence when the signing began (Syropoulos)

people.name: The Georgian envoys, a bishop and a lay prince
people.part: Neither signed; both slipped away (Syropoulos)

people.name: Constantine, catholicos of the Armenians
people.part: Not present; sent the Armenian envoys (Issaverdens)

people.name: Sargis and Joachim
people.part: Armenian envoys named in the catholicos's mandate (Raynaldus)

people.name: Andrew, abbot of Saint Antony's
people.part: Envoy of the Coptic patriarch John; accepted Cantate Domino; also called the Ethiopian emperor's envoy in Eugenius's letter

people.name: John, Coptic patriarch
people.part: Not present; sent Andrew (Cantate Domino, in Raynaldus)

people.name: Zara Yaqob
people.part: Ethiopian emperor; not present; named as sender of the envoys by Eugenius's letter, Patrizi and Perruchon, but not by Dillmann

people.name: Nicodemus, abbot of the Ethiopians in Jerusalem
people.part: Not present; sent the Ethiopian monks, by Dillmann's view as Perruchon reports it

people.name: Abdallah, archbishop of Edessa
people.part: Envoy of Ignatius, patriarch of the Syrians; accepted the faith at the Lateran in 1444 (Raynaldus)

people.name: Timothy, metropolitan of the Chaldeans
people.part: From Cyprus; professed the faith at the Lateran in 1445 (Raynaldus)

people.name: Isaac
people.part: Envoy of Elias, bishop of the Maronites of Cyprus, in 1445 (Raynaldus)

people.name: Ambrogio Traversari
people.part: Signed the decree as Ambrose, general of the Camaldolese (the signed list)

people.name: Basil II of Moscow
people.part: Grand prince; not present; rejected Isidore and the union (Mouravieff; Harasiewicz)

people.name: Jonah of Moscow
people.part: Not present; chosen metropolitan after the years without one that followed Isidore, by Mouravieff

uncertain: Basel's session records are not among our sources, save where Raynaldus, Glassberger and others quote them. Mansi's tomus 31 prints some of Basel's own documents: letters, the Compacts with the Bohemians, John of Ragusa's report and bulls of Felix V. For Ferrara and Florence we hold the Greek acts, a delegate's record, and the decrees with their signatures. The scene at Ferrara comes from Syropoulos, a delegate who signed but wrote against the union.
How Joseph greeted the pope: Syropoulos says he refused the foot-kiss and was received in the pope's room before the cardinals alone. The Greek acts say only that he kissed the pope's cheek.

Who refused to sign: Doukas says all the Greeks agreed except Mark, and Mouravieff says Mark alone did not sign. Syropoulos says Isaias of Stauropolis slipped away rather than sign, and neither Georgian envoy signed. No Stauropolis signature is in the printed list.
The day Joseph died: 9 June 1439 in the Greek acts; 10 June in Syropoulos and in the notes to Doukas. Doukas puts his death "after the union"; the acts and Syropoulos put it before the signing.
Joseph's written statement: the Greek acts say it was found after his death. Mark says the patriarch had long since been corrupted. No held line of Syropoulos says the note was written for him.
The date of the bull moving the council to Ferrara: 18 September 1437 by Raynaldus and Mansi. The acts Justiniani printed read 1 October, which Mansi calls a mistake.
The year the council moved to Rome: Patrizi gives 1442; Mansi argues 1441.
When the council ended: Denzinger's heading gives 1445 and Mansi's tomus 35 gives 1446. No held act names a closing session.
The day of Basel's first session: Glassberger says Friday 7 December 1431. His Quaracchi editors give 14 December, after Hergenröther and Brück.
Felix V's election day, 17 November 1439, rests on Glassberger alone.
The Armenian decree is dated 22 November 1439 in its own dating clause. Raynaldus's narrative puts the Armenians' acceptance in a session of 10 December.
The Coptic decree is dated 4 February 1441 in Denzinger and Mirbt, counting the Florentine year. Mansi gives it as 1442 by our reckoning.

Who sent the Ethiopians: Eugenius's letter, Patrizi and Perruchon name the emperor, Zara Yaqob. Pope Innocent X's brief of 1645, printed by Beccari, also names the king, as Zerah. Alphonsus Mendez, the Catholic patriarch sent to Ethiopia, gave an oration there in 1626. In Almeida's Portuguese of it, the emperor and the patriarch sent them. Ludolf's Latin of the same oration has "your metropolitan" instead. The oration adds that the emperor David later said he still had Eugenius's letter. Dillmann, as Perruchon reports, says Nicodemus of the Ethiopian convent in Jerusalem sent them, without the king's knowledge. Mendez's own history speaks of monks who came to the Florentine synod. Almeida's history says only that some Ethiopians came with the Armenians as the council ended. Catholic writers, Ludolf says, hold that the king's envoys came to Eugenius at Florence. Ludolf answers that nothing of the kind was done at the council. The Jesuits themselves, he says, show that Zara Yaqob stood apart from the Roman church. Beccari, the modern editor of Mendez and Almeida, says historians know Zara Yaqob's obedience at Florence to be a fiction.
The synod of 1443 in which the eastern patriarchs condemn the union: Mansi prints it and thinks it forged; Mouravieff tells it as fact.

Why the Greeks came: that they sought military help is a witness's view. Mark speaks of the city guarded "by the Pope's gold." The Greek chronicle printed by Bekker says no help came, and Mouravieff says no western ruler helped. No decree states a bargain.
How many were at Basel's deposition session: Raynaldus says seven bishops; Aeneas Silvius, as he quotes him, describes how few came. Both reach us through the papal side.
The day of the solemn opening with the Greeks: the Greek acts say Wednesday 9 April 1438; Petit calls it Tuesday.
The Georgian party: Syropoulos first speaks of two bishops and an envoy, then of one bishop and one lay prince.
The Armenian envoys: Issaverdens says four vardapets; the catholicos's mandate in Raynaldus names two.
The Russian rejection rests on Mouravieff, writing in 1838, and Harasiewicz, writing in 1862. No Russian text of the time is among our sources.

Whether Basel stayed a council after the transfer is told by party. Glassberger's editors and the Fifth Lateran Council say it did not. The Lausanne decree and Felix V say it did. In 1446 Eugenius received Basel "from its beginning up to the transfer made by us," Bannwart notes.
